title: Verhandeln und überzeugen / Negotiate and persuade
bridge: In Spanish, politeness and persuasion are often expressed with the subjunctive ('Si me lo permitieras...') or conditionals ('Podríamos...'). In German, in addition to using the Konjunktiv II ('könnte', 'würde'), modal particles such as 'doch', 'mal', 'ja' are used to soften the force of a request without a direct equivalent in Spanish. Caution: the word order in subordinate clauses (verb at the end) and the position of the verb in the main clause can change the strength of the argument. Also avoid translating 'no sé si...' literally as 'ich weiß nicht, ob...', which sounds hesitant in German.
rule: To negotiate and persuade in German at B2 level, use: 1) The Konjunktiv II of modal and auxiliary verbs: 'könnte' (could), 'würde' (would), 'hätte' (would have). It is formed with the past tense of the indicative + ending (or 'würde' + infinitive). 2) Modal particles: 'doch', 'mal', 'ja', 'vielleicht' to soften requests or add emphasis. For example, 'Könnten Sie das mal überlegen?' (Could you consider that?). 3) Polite structures: 'Ich würde vorschlagen...' (I would suggest...), 'Hätten Sie vielleicht...?' (Would you perhaps...?). 4) To concede: 'Wenn Sie ... würden, dann ...' (If you... then...). 5) Modal verbs in Konjunktiv II: 'sollte' (should), 'müsste' (would have to). Remember: in main clauses, the conjugated verb goes in second position, and in subordinate clauses with 'wenn' or 'dass', the verb goes at the end. Avoid the direct imperative in formal contexts; use the polite 'Sie'.

title: Meinung äußern und begründen / Expressing and justifying opinions in depth
bridge: In Spanish, we often use connectors like 'pienso que', 'en mi opinión' and justifications with 'porque'. In German, in addition to 'ich denke, dass', it is very common to use constructions with 'nämlich', 'da' and structures like 'was ... anbelangt'. A key point is that in German modal verbs and subordinating conjunctions change the word order, which does not happen in Spanish. Another important difference is that in German 'meiner Meinung nach' is used with the dative, and the position of the verb in the main clause can vary. Pay attention to the position of the verb when introducing an opinion with 'dass'.
rule:
To express and justify opinions in German at B2 level, you need to master:
1) Verbs and expressions of opinion: 'ich denke, ich finde, ich glaube, meiner Meinung nach, ich bin der Ansicht, ich bin überzeugt'. Examples: 'Ich denke, dass...', 'Meiner Meinung nach ist...'.
2) Connectors for justification: 'weil' (because), 'da' (since), 'nämlich' (it's that), 'denn' (as). Remember: 'weil' and 'da' send the verb to the end of the subordinate clause, while 'denn' does not alter the order and is used in coordinated clauses.
3) For nuances: 'obwohl' (although), 'trotzdem' (nevertheless), 'allerdings' (however), 'einerseits... andererseits' (on the one hand... on the other).
4) Structures for emphasis: 'Was ... anbelangt' (as far as ... is concerned), 'In Bezug auf' (with regard to).
Example of complex justification: 'Obwohl die Kosten höher sind, bin ich der Meinung, dass die Qualität besser ist.' (Although the costs are higher, I think the quality is better).

title: Über die Vergangenheit spekulieren / Speculating about the past
bridge: In Spanish you use the compound conditional (habría + past participle) to speculate about the past, for example: 'Habría llegado tarde'. In German, the equivalent form is the Konjunktiv II of the auxiliary verbs haben and sein with the past participle: 'Er wäre zu spät gekommen'. However, there are two key differences: first, the auxiliary verb chosen depends on the main verb (sein with verbs of movement and change of state, haben with the rest); second, the position of the auxiliary verb is at the end of the subordinate clause, and the verb with sein goes with the past participle that already includes the ge- prefix. Additionally, in German it is common to use 'hätte' (would have) with modal verbs in constructions like 'hätte machen können' (would have been able to do), where the modal appears in the infinitive at the end, which contrasts with the Spanish structure. Be careful not to directly copy the Spanish structure of 'habría + past participle', as in German you need the Konjunktiv II of the auxiliary and the correct placement.
rule: To speculate about the past in German, the Konjunktiv II of the auxiliary verbs (haben/sein) + past participle (Partizip II) of the main verb is used, and in subordinate clauses the auxiliary goes at the end. The formula is: [Konjunktiv II of haben/sein] + [Partizip II] (in main clauses, the conjugated auxiliary goes in position 2). The Konjunktiv II of 'haben' is 'hätte' (for all persons: ich hätte, du hättest, er/sie/es hätte, wir hätten, ihr hättet, sie/Sie hätten). The Konjunktiv II of 'sein' is 'wäre' (ich wäre, du wärest, er/sie/es wäre, wir wären, ihr wäret, sie/Sie wären). 'Sein' is used as an auxiliary when the main verb indicates movement (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen) or change of state (werden, sterben, aufwachen, einschlafen). In all other cases, 'haben' is used. Examples: 'Er wäre gekommen' (He would have come), 'Wir hätten es gemacht' (We would have done it). To express speculation about the past with modal verbs, the construction is: Konjunktiv II of haben + past participle of the modal + infinitive of the main verb (often in infinitive). Example: 'Er hätte kommen können' (He would have been able to come). The Konjunktiv II of haben + past participle + zu + infinitive is also used for passive constructions or with 'lassen' (e.g., 'Das hätte gemacht werden müssen' - That would have had to be done). In sentences with 'als ob' (as if), the past Konjunktiv II is used: 'Er tut so, als ob er es gewusst hätte' (He acts as if he had known it). The use of 'würde + haben/sein + past participle' is not correct for the past; for the past, hätte/wäre must always be used. In colloquial German, sometimes 'hätte' is used instead of 'wäre' with verbs of movement, but it is considered incorrect in standard German. Pay attention to the position of the verb in the subordinate clause with 'dass' or in structures with 'wenn'.

common_error.explanation: The error is using 'würde + infinitive' to express speculation about the past. 'Würde' is only used for the conditional in the present or future (e.g., 'Er würde kommen' = He would come). For the past, it is mandatory to use 'wäre' (Konjunktiv II of sein) or 'hätte' (of haben). The form 'würde gestern kommen' sounds like future in the past, not a speculation about a past event. To correct it, either use 'wäre + past participle' (Er wäre gekommen) or, if you want to emphasize possibility, 'hätte + past participle + können'.

title: Abstrakte Konzepte diskutieren / Discuss abstract concepts
bridge: In German, abstract concepts are frequently expressed using modal verbs ('können', 'sollen', 'müssen', 'dürfen') and modal particles (such as 'ja', 'doch', 'eben', 'halt') that add nuance to the sentence in ways that in Spanish are conveyed through intonation or words like 'precisely', 'actually', 'of course'. The subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) is also commonly used for hypotheses and advice, which in Spanish corresponds to the conditional. A typical error for Spanish speakers is omitting these particles or translating structures like 'me parece que' ('ich denke, dass') literally without the nuance of opinion that the Konjunktiv II requires.
rule: To discuss abstract concepts in German at B2 level: 1) Use the Konjunktiv II of modal verbs and of 'haben' and 'sein' to express possibilities or hypothetical conditions (e.g., 'könnte', 'würde', 'hätte', 'wäre'). 2) Use modal particles ('ja', 'doch', 'eben', 'halt', 'eigentlich') to modulate the discourse; these are not translated literally but interpreted according to context. 3) Use nominalizations (e.g., 'die Freiheit', 'das Bewusstsein') to refer to abstract concepts, often with the neuter article 'das' + substantivized infinitive (e.g., 'das Denken'). 4) In general statements, word order is flexible, but the conjugated verb always occupies position 2; in subordinate clauses, the verb goes at the end. 5) Connectors such as 'obwohl', 'während', 'sofern' help express logical relationships. Pay attention to the gender of abstract nouns: many feminine nouns end in '-heit', '-keit', '-ung', '-schaft', and many neuter nouns in '-um', '-nis' (though some have exceptions).

concept_examples.text: Man könnte sagen, dass Freiheit immer mit Verantwortung verbunden ist.
concept_examples.translation: One could say that freedom is always related to responsibility.
concept_examples.phonetic: /man ˈkœntə ˈzaːɡən das ˈfʁaɪ̯haɪ̯t ˈɪmɐ mɪt fɛɐ̯ˈʔantvɔʁtʊŋ fɛɐ̯ˈbʊndn̩ ɪst/

concept_examples.text: Es ist eigentlich schwer, das Konzept der Gerechtigkeit zu definieren.
concept_examples.translation: Actually, it is difficult to define the concept of justice.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛs ɪst ˈaɪ̯ɡəntlɪç ʃveːɐ̯ das kɔnˈt͡sɛpt deːɐ̯ ɡəˈʁɛçtɪçaɪ̯t tsuː defiˈniːʁən/

concept_examples.text: Wenn man über das Bewusstsein nachdenkt, entdeckt man viele Paradoxien.
concept_examples.translation: When one thinks about consciousness, many paradoxes emerge.
concept_examples.phonetic: /vɛn man ˈyːbɐ das bəˈvʊstzaɪ̯n ˈnaːxdɛŋkt ɛntˈdɛkt man ˈfiːlə paʁaˈdɔksi̯ən/

concept_examples.text: Die Wahrheit kann manchmal wehtun, aber sie ist wichtig für die Gesellschaft.
concept_examples.translation: The truth can sometimes hurt, but it is important for society.
concept_examples.phonetic: /diː ˈvaːɐ̯haɪ̯t kan ˈmanʃmaːl ˈveːtuːn ˈaːbɐ ziː ɪst ˈvɪçtɪç fyːɐ̯ diː ɡəˈzɛlʃaft/

common_error.wrong: Ich denke, dass die Freiheit ist wichtig.
common_error.correct: Ich denke, dass die Freiheit wichtig ist.
common_error.correct_alt: Meiner Meinung nach ist die Freiheit wichtig.
common_error.explanation: The error lies in the position of the verb in the subordinate clause introduced by 'dass': in German, the conjugated verb must come at the end of the subordinate clause, unlike in Spanish where it follows the subject. Additionally, 'Ich denke' + 'dass' is not always the most appropriate form; phrases like 'Meiner Meinung nach' or 'Ich bin der Ansicht, dass' can sound more natural in abstract contexts.

examples.original: Meiner Ansicht nach ist Glück kein Zufall.
examples.phonetic: /ˈmaɪ̯nɐ ˈanzɪçt naːx ɪst ɡlʏk kaɪ̯n ˈt͡suːfal/
examples.translation: In my opinion, happiness is not a matter of chance.
examples.note: The expression 'meiner Ansicht nach' is equivalent to 'in my opinion' and requires the verb in position 2, not after the introductory phrase.

examples.original: Es lässt sich sagen, dass Fortschritt oft mit Verlust einhergeht.
examples.phonetic: /ɛs lɛst zɪç ˈzaːɡən das ˈfɔʁtʃʁɪt ɔft mɪt fɛɐ̯ˈlʊst ˈaɪ̯nhɐɡeːt/
examples.translation: One could say that progress often entails loss.
examples.note: The construction 'es lässt sich sagen' is an impersonal way to express an opinion, equivalent to 'one could say' in Spanish.

examples.original: Ich würde behaupten, dass Kultur immer im Wandel ist.
examples.phonetic: /ɪç ˈvʏʁdə bəˈhaʊ̯ptn̩ das kʊlˈtuːɐ̯ ˈɪmɐ ɪm ˈvandl̩ ɪst/
examples.translation: I would say that culture is always changing.
examples.note: The Konjunktiv II of 'würde' + infinitive ('würde behaupten') softens the statement, similar to the conditional in Spanish.

examples.original: Wenn es keine Regeln gäbe, wäre die Gesellschaft chaotisch.
examples.phonetic: /vɛn ɛs ˈkaɪ̯nə ˈʁeːɡl̩n ˈɡɛːbə ˈvɛːʁə diː ɡəˈzɛlʃaft kaˈoːtɪʃ/
examples.translation: If there were no rules, society would be chaotic.
examples.note: This unreal conditional uses the Konjunktiv II (gäbe, wäre) just as 'hubiera' and 'sería' are used in Spanish.

examples.original: Man könnte argumentieren, dass Technologie die menschliche Kreativität einschränkt.
examples.phonetic: /man ˈkœntə aʁɡumɛnˈtiːʁən das tɛçnoloˈɡiː diː ˈmɛnʃlɪçə kʁeativiˈtɛːt ˈaɪ̯nʃʁɛŋkt/
examples.translation: One could argue that technology limits human creativity.
examples.note: The modal 'könnte' in Konjunktiv II expresses possibility, equivalent to 'could' in Spanish.

examples.original: Es wäre denkbar, dass sich die Werte in der Zukunft ändern.
examples.phonetic: /ɛs ˈvɛːʁə ˈdɛŋkbaːɐ̯ das zɪç diː ˈveːɐ̯tə ɪn deːɐ̯ ˈt͡suːkʊnft ˈɛndɐn/
examples.translation: It would be conceivable that values change in the future.
examples.note: The construction 'es wäre denkbar' is useful for posing hypotheses; it requires the subjunctive in the subordinate clause.

examples.original: Das ist eine Frage der Perspektive.
examples.phonetic: /das ɪst ˈaɪ̯nə ˈfʁaːɡə deːɐ̯ pɛʁspɛkˈtiːvə/
examples.translation: It is a matter of perspective.
examples.note: The structure 'eine Frage + Genitiv' is common for expressing abstract concepts; in Spanish, 'una cuestión de' is used.

examples.original: Seine Theorie basiert auf der Annahme, dass alles relativ ist.
examples.phonetic: /ˈzaɪ̯nə teoˈʁiː baˈziːɐ̯t aʊ̯f deːɐ̯ ˈanˌnaːmə das ˈaləs ʁelaˈtiːf ɪst/
examples.translation: Their theory is based on the assumption that everything is relative.
examples.note: The noun 'Annahme' (assumption) requires the feminine article and is used with the preposition 'auf' followed by the dative case.

examples.original: Das Individuum steht oft im Konflikt mit der kollektiven Identität.
examples.phonetic: /das ˈɪndividuːm ʃteːt ɔft ɪm kɔnˈflɪkt mɪt deːɐ̯ kɔlɛkˈtiːvən idɛntiˈtɛːt/
examples.translation: The individual is often in conflict with collective identity.
examples.note: The plural 'Individuum' and many abstract words of Latin origin retain their original form; pay attention to the neuter gender.

title: Nuancen komplexer Gefühle ausdrücken / Express complex emotions with nuances
bridge: In Spanish, we often use verbs like 'sentir' or 'estar' with adjectives, but in German, emotional nuances are often expressed using modal verbs, modal particles (ja, doch, wohl), and structures like 'es macht mich...' or 'ich bin...'. A common mistake is to translate 'me siento frustrado' literally as 'ich fühle mich frustriert', but in German it is more natural to say 'ich bin frustriert' or 'es frustriert mich'. Additionally, adjectives with prefixes like 'über-' or 'unter-' change the intensity ('überglücklich' vs. 'glücklich'), which has no direct equivalent in Spanish. Pay attention to the placement of 'mir' in the dative case in expressions like 'es ist mir peinlich' (it embarrasses me), which differs from the Spanish structure.
rule: To express complex emotions in German at the B2 level, use: 1) Adjectives with intensifying prefixes: 'überglücklich' (overjoyed), 'tiefbetrübt' (deeply sad), 'hocherfreut' (very pleased). 2) Constructions with 'es' + dative + adjective: 'es ist mir peinlich' (it embarrasses me), 'es ist mir unangenehm' (it feels uncomfortable to me). 3) Modal verbs with emotional weight: 'ich könnte schreien' (I want to scream, out of frustration), 'ich kann nicht mehr' (I can’t take it anymore). 4) Modal particles to nuance meaning: 'Das ist ja wohl kaum zu glauben' (that’s hardly believable), where 'ja' and 'wohl' soften or strengthen the statement. 5) Subordinate clauses with 'dass' to explain feelings: 'Es macht mich traurig, dass...' (it makes me sad that...). Pay attention to the use of the subjunctive II for wishes or hypothetical situations related to emotions: 'Ich wäre so erleichtert, wenn...' (I would be so relieved if...). Avoid the literal translation of 'sentirse' as 'sich fühlen' when German simply uses 'sein' or 'werden'.

concept_examples.text: Ich bin überglücklich, dass du gekommen bist.
concept_examples.translation: I’m overjoyed that you came.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɪç bɪn ˈyːbɐˌɡlʏklɪç das duː ˈɡɛkɔmən bɪst]

concept_examples.text: Es ist mir peinlich, das zuzugeben.
concept_examples.translation: I’m embarrassed to admit it.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɛs ɪst miːɐ̯ ˈpaɪ̯nlɪç das ˈtsuːtsuːɡeːbən]

concept_examples.text: Ich könnte vor Wut schreien.
concept_examples.translation: I could scream with rage.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɪç ˈkœntə foːɐ̯ vuːt ˈʃʁaɪ̯ən]

concept_examples.text: Es macht mich traurig, dass ihr geht.
concept_examples.translation: It saddens me that you’re leaving.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɛs maxt mɪç ˈtʁaʊ̯ʁɪç das iːɐ̯ geːt]

common_error.wrong: Ich fühle mich frustriert wegen der Situation.
common_error.correct: Ich bin frustriert wegen der Situation.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'me siento frustrado' is literally translated as 'ich fühle mich frustriert', but in German it is more idiomatic to use 'ich bin' + adjective or the transitive verb 'frustrieren'. The use of 'sich fühlen' sounds overly reflexive and unnatural in everyday emotional contexts. Avoid literal translations and opt for more direct structures. Additionally, 'wegen' is used correctly, but the adjective 'frustriert' must be placed immediately after 'bin'.

examples.original: Sie war tiefbetrübt nach der Nachricht.
examples.phonetic: [ziː vaːɐ̯ tiːfbəˈtʁyːpt naːx deːɐ̯ ˈnaːxʁɪçt]
examples.translation: She was deeply sad after the news.
examples.note: The prefix 'tief-' intensifies the adjective 'betrübt' (sad). In Spanish, there is no equivalent prefix, so it is translated with an adverb.

examples.original: Er ist hocherfreut über deine Einladung.
examples.phonetic: [eːɐ̯ ɪst ˈhoːxʔɛɐ̯ˌfʁɔɪ̯t ˈyːbɐ ˈdaɪ̯nə ˈaɪ̯nlaːdʊŋ]
examples.translation: He is very pleased with your invitation.
examples.note: 'Hocherfreut' is a formal adjective, often used in written or formal contexts. In Spanish, we use 'muy complacido'.

examples.original: Ich bin überglücklich über die gute Note.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç bɪn ˈyːbɐɡlʏklɪç ˈyːbɐ diː ɡuːtə ˈnoːtə]
examples.translation: I’m overjoyed about the good grade.
examples.note: The prefix 'über-' indicates an extreme degree. It is used with positive adjectives like 'glücklich'.

examples.original: Es ist mir unangenehm, darüber zu sprechen.
examples.phonetic: [ɛs ɪst miːɐ̯ ˈʊnʔanɡəneːm daˈʁyːbɐ tsuː ˈʃpʁɛçən]
examples.translation: It feels uncomfortable to me to talk about that.
examples.note: The pronoun 'mir' is in the dative case and comes after the verb 'ist'. In Spanish, we use 'me resulta' or 'me es'.

examples.original: Es war ihm peinlich, dass er weinte.
examples.phonetic: [ɛs vaːɐ̯ iːm ˈpaɪ̯nlɪç das eːɐ̯ ˈvaɪ̯ntə]
examples.translation: He was embarrassed that she cried.
examples.note: In German, the emotion is expressed with 'es' as the subject and the person in the dative case. In Spanish, we use the verb 'dar' with 'vergüenza'.

examples.original: Es ist uns wichtig, dass du ehrlich bist.
examples.phonetic: [ɛs ɪst ʊns ˈvɪçtɪç das duː ˈeːɐ̯lɪç bɪst]
examples.translation: It is important to us that you are honest.
examples.note: This structure is also used for feelings related to values, not just strong emotions.

examples.original: Ich könnte heulen vor Freude.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç ˈkœntə ˈhɔɪ̯lən foːɐ̯ ˈfʁɔɪ̯də]
examples.translation: I could cry with joy.
examples.note: The subjunctive II of 'können' (könnte) expresses an intense emotional reaction. In Spanish, we use 'podría' or 'podría + infinitive'.

examples.original: Du kannst dir nicht vorstellen, wie aufgeregt ich bin.
examples.phonetic: [duː kanst diːɐ̯ nɪçt ˈfoːɐ̯ʃtɛlən viː ˈaʊ̯fɡəʁeːkt ɪç bɪn]
examples.translation: You can’t imagine how excited I am.
examples.note: The modal verb 'können' in the negative expresses disbelief or emotional intensity.

examples.original: Ich will nicht mehr weiterreden.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç vɪl nɪçt meːɐ̯ ˈvaɪ̯tɐˌʁeːdən]
examples.translation: I don’t want to keep talking anymore.
examples.note: The modal 'wollen' in the negative expresses emotional rejection, often due to frustration or exhaustion.

title: Formal Written Communication: Reports and Emails / Formal Writing: Reports and Emails
bridge: In Spanish, formal politeness is often expressed with the subjunctive and phrases like 'Le agradecería' or 'Quedo a su disposición'. In German, formality is primarily marked by consistent use of 'Sie' (capitalized), verb-final construction in subordinate clauses, and the Konjunktiv II (würde, hätte, wäre) for polite nuances. A common error is directly transferring Spanish word order, forgetting that German verb position is strictly governed by sentence type. Additionally, formal greetings and closings have no direct equivalent; for example, 'Mit freundlichen Grüßen' does not translate literally to Spanish.
rule: To write formal reports and emails in German at B2 level: 1) Formal greeting: 'Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren' (if name unknown) or 'Sehr geehrte Frau/Herr [Nachname]' (with name). 2) Body: Use 'Sie' (always capitalized) for formal address. Maintain verb-second position in main clauses and verb-final in subordinate clauses (e.g., with 'dass', 'weil', 'obwohl'). Use Konjunktiv II for polite requests: 'Ich würde Sie bitten...' or 'Es wäre hilfreich, wenn...' 3) Closing: 'Mit freundlichen Grüßen' (equivalent to 'Atentamente'). Avoid contractions (no 'im' in very formal contexts; write 'in dem' if necessary). 4) Report structure: introduction (Einleitung), body (Hauptteil), conclusion (Schlussfolgerung), and recommendations (Empfehlungen). 5) Formal connectors: 'Darüber hinaus', 'Des Weiteren', 'In Bezug auf', 'Zusammenfassend'.

concept_examples.text: Sehr geehrte Frau Müller, ich schreibe Ihnen bezüglich Ihrer Anfrage vom 15. März.
concept_examples.translation: Dear Ms. Müller, I am writing to you regarding your inquiry from March 15th.
concept_examples.phonetic: [zeːɐ̯ ɡəˈeːɐ̯tə fʁaʊ̯ ˈmʏlɐ, ɪç ˈʃʁaɪ̯bə ˈiːnən bəˈt͡sʏklɪç ˈiːʁɐ ˈanfʁaːɡə fɔm ˈfʏnft͡seːntən ˈmɛʁt͡s]

concept_examples.text: Wir möchten Sie darüber informieren, dass die Besprechung auf nächste Woche verschoben wurde.
concept_examples.translation: We would like to inform you that the meeting has been postponed until next week.
concept_examples.phonetic: [vɪʁ ˈmœçtən ziː daˈʁyːbɐ ɪnfɔʁˈmiːʁən, das diː bəˈʃpʁɛçʊŋ aʊ̯f ˈnɛːçstə ˈvɔxə fɛɐ̯ˈʃoːbən ˈvʊʁdə]

concept_examples.text: Es wäre sehr hilfreich, wenn Sie uns die Unterlagen bis Ende der Woche zusenden könnten.
concept_examples.translation: It would be of great help if you could send us the documents by the weekend.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɛs ˈvɛːʁə zeːɐ̯ ˈhɪlfʁaɪ̯ç, vɛn ziː ʊns diː ˈʊntɐlaːɡən bɪs ˈɛndə deːɐ̯ ˈvɔxə ˈt͡suːzɛndən ˈkœntən]

concept_examples.text: Für weitere Fragen stehe ich Ihnen gerne zur Verfügung.
concept_examples.translation: Should you have any further questions, I remain at your disposal.
concept_examples.phonetic: [fyːɐ̯ ˈvaɪ̯təʁə fʁaːɡən ˈʃteːə ɪç ˈiːnən ˈɡɛʁnə t͡suːɐ̯ fɛɐ̯ˈfyːɡʊŋ]

common_error.wrong: Ich schreibe Ihnen, ich brauche die Informationen.
common_error.correct: Ich schreibe Ihnen, weil ich die Informationen benötige.
common_error.correct_alt: Ich schreibe Ihnen, da ich die Informationen benötige.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, it is common to join two sentences with a comma without an explicit conjunction, but in formal German, a subordinating conjunction like 'weil' or 'da' is required, which forces the verb to the end of the subordinate clause. Additionally, in formal contexts, 'benötigen' is preferred over 'brauchen', which is more colloquial.

examples.original: Sehr geehrter Herr Schmidt, vielen Dank für Ihre schnelle Antwort.
examples.phonetic: [zeːɐ̯ ɡəˈeːɐ̯tɐ hɛʁ ʃmɪt, ˈfiːlən daŋk fyːɐ̯ ˈiːʁə ˈʃnɛlə ˈantvɔʁt]
examples.translation: Dear Mr. Schmidt, thank you very much for your prompt response.
examples.note: Use 'Sehr geehrter' for men and 'Sehr geehrte' for women, followed by Herr/Frau and the surname.

examples.original: ich melde mich bezüglich Ihrer Stellenausschreibung.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç ˈmɛldə mɪç bəˈt͡sʏklɪç ˈiːʁɐ ˈʃtɛlənʔaʊ̯sʃʁaɪ̯bʊŋ]
examples.translation: I am contacting you regarding your job offer.
examples.note: In German, the main clause begins with 'ich', but the verb 'melde' must be in second position.

examples.original: Mit Bezug auf unser Telefonat vom letzten Dienstag...
examples.phonetic: [mɪt bəˈt͡suːk aʊ̯f ˈʊnzɐ telefoˈnaːt fɔm ˈlɛt͡stən ˈdiːnstaːk]
examples.translation: With reference to our telephone conversation from last Tuesday...
examples.note: This phrase is useful for starting a letter by referencing prior contact.

examples.original: Könnten Sie mir bitte die genauen Daten mitteilen?
examples.phonetic: [ˈkœntən ziː miːɐ̯ ˈbɪtə diː ɡəˈnaʊ̯ən ˈdaːtən ˈmɪttaɪlən]
examples.translation: Could you please provide me with the exact details?
examples.note: The Konjunktiv II 'könnten' softens the request and is more polite than 'können'.

examples.original: Ich wäre Ihnen dankbar, wenn Sie die Anlage prüfen würden.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç ˈvɛːʁə ˈiːnən ˈdaŋkbaːɐ̯, vɛn ziː diː ˈanlaːɡə ˈpʁyːfən ˈvʏʁdən]
examples.translation: I would appreciate it if you could review the attachment.
examples.note: The structure with 'wenn' + Konjunktiv II is typical for polite requests; the verb goes at the end.

examples.original: Es würde uns freuen, Sie bald bei uns begrüßen zu dürfen.
examples.phonetic: [ɛs ˈvʏʁdə ʊns ˈfʁɔʏən, ziː balt baɪ̯ ʊns bəˈɡʁyːsən t͡suː ˈdʏʁfən]
examples.translation: We would be happy to welcome you soon.
examples.note: The construction 'würde + infinitive' is common for expressing formal wishes.

examples.original: Bitte senden Sie uns die Unterlagen umgehend zurück.
examples.phonetic: [ˈbɪtə ˈzɛndən ziː ʊns diː ˈʊntɐlaːɡən ˈʊmɡeːənt t͡suːˈʁʏk]
examples.translation: Please return the documents to us immediately.
examples.note: In formal imperative, the 'Sie' form is used with the verb in initial position.

examples.original: Für Rückfragen stehe ich Ihnen selbstverständlich zur Verfügung.
examples.phonetic: [fyːɐ̯ ˈʁʏkfʁaːɡən ˈʃteːə ɪç ˈiːnən ˈzɛlpstfɛɐ̯ˌʃtɛntlɪç t͡suːɐ̯ fɛɐ̯ˈfyːɡʊŋ]
examples.translation: Of course, I remain at your disposal for any questions.
examples.note: This phrase is typical for closing the body of the email.

examples.original: Ich bedanke mich im Voraus für Ihre Bemühungen.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç bəˈdaŋkə mɪç ɪm foˈʁaʊ̯s fyːɐ̯ ˈiːʁə bəˈmyːʊŋən]
examples.translation: Thank you in advance for your efforts.
examples.note: Used to express gratitude before an action takes place, common in requests.

examples.original: Mit freundlichen Grüßen
examples.phonetic: [mɪt ˈfʁɔɪ̯ntlɪçən ˈɡʁyːsən]
examples.translation: Sincerely (literal: With friendly greetings)
examples.note: This is the standard closing in formal emails. It should not be literally translated as 'with friendly greetings' in Spanish.

examples.original: Hochachtungsvoll
examples.phonetic: [ˈhoːxʔaxtʊŋsfɔl]
examples.translation: Respectfully (very elevated formality)
examples.note: Used in highly formal contexts such as letters to authorities, but less common in emails.

title: Conflict resolution / Managing conflicts
bridge: In Spanish, we often use the subjunctive or constructions like 'quizás' (maybe) or 'no sé si' (I don’t know if) to soften criticism. In German, the Konjunktiv II and modal verbs in the past tense (sollte, könnte, müsste) are essential for expressing suggestions or complaints politely. A common mistake is using the indicative directly, which sounds too harsh. You’ll also notice that German uses 'würde' + infinitive more frequently than the proper subjunctive.
rule: To manage conflicts in German at level B2, the following are primarily used: 1) Konjunktiv II of modal verbs: sollte (should), könnte (could), müsste (would have to) for soft suggestions or complaints. 2) Konjunktiv II of haben/sein: hätte (would have), wäre (would be) for hypothetical situations. 3) The form 'würde + infinitive' for hypothetical actions or polite requests (though in formal contexts, the Konjunktiv II of common verbs is preferred). 4) Expressions such as 'Ich finde, dass...' (I think that...), 'Es wäre besser, wenn...' (it would be better if...), 'Könntest du bitte...' (could you please...). In conditional sentences, 'wenn' + Konjunktiv II is used, and in indirect speech to convey criticism, Konjunktiv I is employed (though at B2 level, Konjunktiv II can be used in informal contexts). The word order in main clauses is verb in second position, and in subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb comes at the end. Remember that 'Sie' is formal, 'du' is informal; using 'du' requires specific verb forms (kannst, sollst, etc.).

concept_examples.text: Ich finde, dass wir das anders lösen sollten.
concept_examples.translation: I think we should resolve this differently.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈfɪndə das vɪʁ das ˈandɐs ˈløːzn̩ ˈzɔltn̩

concept_examples.text: Könntest du bitte leiser sprechen?
concept_examples.translation: Could you please speak more quietly?
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈkœntəst duː ˈbɪtə ˈlaɪzɐ ˈʃpʁɛçn̩

concept_examples.text: Es wäre besser, wenn du das noch einmal überdenken würdest.
concept_examples.translation: It would be better if you reconsidered one more time.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɛs ˈvɛːʁə ˈbɛsɐ vɛn duː das nɔx ˈaɪnmaːl ˌyːbɐˈdɛŋkən ˈvyːdəst

concept_examples.text: Ich hätte einen Vorschlag, wie wir das Problem lösen könnten.
concept_examples.translation: I’d have a suggestion on how we could resolve the problem.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈhɛtə ˈaɪnən ˈfoːʁʃlaːk viː viːɐ̯ das pʁoˈbleːm ˈløːzn̩ ˈkœntn̩

common_error.wrong: Ich will, dass du leiser sprichst.
common_error.correct: Ich möchte, dass du leiser sprichst.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'quiero que' (I want that) is common, but in German, 'will' (from wollen) sounds very authoritarian and harsh. For a polite request, 'möchte' (would like) or the Konjunktiv II 'könntest du' (could you) is used. Spanish speakers tend to use the indicative or direct subjunctive, but in German, politeness is clearly expressed with Konjunktiv II and modal verbs.

examples.original: Ich bin nicht zufrieden mit der Situation.
examples.phonetic: ɪç bɪn nɪçt tsuˈfʁiːdən mɪt deːɐ̯ zituaˈt͡si̯oːn
examples.translation: I’m not satisfied with the situation.
examples.note: Use 'nicht zufrieden' for a soft complaint. In Spanish, you’d say 'no estoy contento' (I’m not happy).

examples.original: Das ist mir wirklich wichtig, dass wir das klären.
examples.phonetic: das ɪst miːɐ̯ ˈvɪʁklɪç ˈvɪçtɪç das viːɐ̯ das ˈklɛːʁən
examples.translation: It’s really important to me that we clarify this.
examples.note: Emphasize importance without being aggressive. The 'dass' clause places the verb at the end.

examples.original: Ich muss ehrlich sagen, dass ich das anders sehe.
examples.phonetic: ɪç mʊs ˈeːɐ̯lɪç ˈzaːɡən das ɪç das ˈandɐs ˈzeːə
examples.translation: I must honestly say that I see it differently.
examples.note: 'Muss ehrlich sagen' softens the criticism, similar to Spanish 'debo decir que' (I must say that).

examples.original: Wie wäre es, wenn wir uns in der Mitte treffen?
examples.phonetic: viː ˈvɛːʁə ɛs vɛn viːɐ̯ ʊns ɪn deːɐ̯ ˈmɪtə ˈtʁɛfn̩
examples.translation: How would you feel if we met halfway?
examples.note: The construction 'Wie wäre es, wenn' is key for suggestions, equivalent to 'what if...?'.

examples.original: Wir könnten einen Kompromiss eingehen.
examples.phonetic: viːɐ̯ ˈkœntn̩ ˈaɪnən kɔmpʁoˈmɪs ˈaɪnɡeːən
examples.translation: We could reach a compromise.
examples.note: 'Könnten' (we could) expresses possibility and openness to dialogue.

examples.original: Ich schlage vor, dass wir das noch einmal besprechen.
examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈʃlaːɡə foːɐ̯ das viːɐ̯ das nɔx ˈaɪnmaːl bəˈʃpʁɛçən
examples.translation: I suggest we talk about it one more time.
examples.note: The verb 'vorschlagen' (to suggest) is separable; it splits in the main clause: 'schlage...vor'.

examples.original: Okay, du hast recht, ich habe das übersehen.
examples.phonetic: oˈkeː duː hast ʁɛçt ɪç ˈhaːbə das yːbɐˈzeːən
examples.translation: Okay, you’re right, I overlooked it.
examples.note: Acknowledging the mistake: 'du hast recht' (you’re right) is a set phrase. 'Übersehen' (to overlook) is separable, but in the past participle, it doesn’t split.

examples.original: Es tut mir leid, ich hätte anders reagieren sollen.
examples.phonetic: ɛs tuːt miːɐ̯ laɪt ɪç ˈhɛtə ˈandɐs ʁeaˈɡiːʁən ˈzɔlən
examples.translation: I’m sorry, I should have reacted differently.
examples.note: Use of Konjunktiv II with 'hätte' + past participle + modal in infinitive: 'hätte reagieren sollen' (should have reacted).

examples.original: Ich entschuldige mich bei dir für mein Verhalten.
examples.phonetic: ɪç ɛntˈʃʊldɪɡə mɪç baɪ diːɐ̯ fyːɐ̯ maɪn fɛɐ̯ˈhaltən
examples.translation: I apologize to you for my behavior.
examples.note: The verb 'sich entschuldigen' (to apologize) is constructed with 'bei' (to someone) and 'für' (for something).

title: Zusammenfassen und Paraphrasieren / Summarizing and paraphrasing
bridge: In Spanish, when summarizing, we often use indirect speech with tense and person changes, but in German, modal verbs and modal particles (such as 'ja', 'doch') play a crucial role in conveying the speaker's attitude. Additionally, German distinguishes between 'resumir' (zusammenfassen) and 'paraphrase' (umschreiben): while summarizing condenses essential information, paraphrasing reformulates an idea with different words. A common mistake is translating 'según' literally as 'laut', but in German 'laut' is only used with sources, not with personal opinions.
rule: To summarize in German, structures like 'Das bedeutet, dass...' (That means...), 'Im Grunde genommen...' (Basically...), or 'Kurz gesagt...' (In short...) are used. For paraphrasing, expressions such as 'Anders ausgedrückt...' (In other words...), 'Mit anderen Worten...' (Put differently...) are used. In indirect speech, the verb goes into the subjunctive I (er sagte, er habe...), but in colloquial language, the indicative or subjunctive II (hätte, wäre) is often used to avoid ambiguities. When summarizing texts, connectors like 'zunächst' (first), 'dann' (then), 'schließlich' (finally) are employed. It is important to remember that the verb in the subordinate clause goes at the end, and that modal verbs ('können', 'sollen', 'wollen') are used to express possibility, obligation, or intention, respectively.

concept_examples.text: Kurz gesagt, das Projekt war erfolgreich.
concept_examples.translation: In summary, the project was successful.

concept_examples.text: Der Autor behauptet, dass die Wirtschaft wächst.
concept_examples.translation: The author states that the economy is growing.
concept_examples.phonetic: [deːɐ̯ ˈaʊ̯toːɐ̯ bəˈhaʊ̯ptət, das diː ˈvɪʁtʃaft vɛkst]

concept_examples.text: Mit anderen Worten, wir müssen sparen.
concept_examples.translation: In other words, we have to save.
concept_examples.phonetic: [mɪt ˈandɐn ˈvɔʁtən, viːɐ̯ ˈmʏsn̩ ˈʃpaːʁən]

concept_examples.text: Zusammengefasst lässt sich sagen, dass die Lage stabil ist.
concept_examples.translation: In summary, it can be said that the situation is stable.
concept_examples.phonetic: [tsuˈzamənɡəfasst lɛst zɪç ˈzaːɡən, das diː ˈlaːɡə ʃtaˈbiːl ɪst]

common_error.wrong: Según el autor, die Situation ist schwierig.
common_error.correct: Laut dem Autor ist die Situation schwierig.
common_error.correct_alt: Der Autor sagt, dass die Situation schwierig ist.
common_error.explanation: The mistake consists of translating 'según' literally as 'según', which does not exist in German. The correct word is 'laut' + dative, or 'nach' (meiner Meinung nach) can be used. It is also common to place the verb in the correct position: in German, in the main clause the conjugated verb goes in second position, not at the end as in the subordinate clause.

examples.original: Das Wichtigste ist, dass wir pünktlich ankommen.
examples.phonetic: [das ˈvɪçtɪçstə ɪst, das viːɐ̯ ˈpʏŋktlɪç ˈankɔmən]
examples.translation: The most important thing is that we arrive on time.
examples.note: 'das Wichtigste' is used to highlight what is essential when summarizing.

examples.original: Im Großen und Ganzen war die Reise angenehm.
examples.phonetic: [ɪm ˈɡʁoːsn̩ ʊnt ˈɡantsn̩ vaːɐ̯ diː ˈʁaɪ̯zə ˈanɡəneːm]
examples.translation: Overall, the trip was pleasant.
examples.note: Fixed expression for summarizing in a general way.

examples.original: Er sagte, er habe keine Zeit.
examples.phonetic: [eːɐ̯ ˈzaːktə, eːɐ̯ ˈhaːbə ˈkaɪ̯nə tsaɪ̯t]
examples.translation: He said he didn’t have time.
examples.note: Use of the subjunctive I 'habe' for indirect speech.

examples.original: Sie meint, die Preise könnten steigen.
examples.phonetic: [ziː maɪ̯nt, diː ˈpʁaɪ̯zə ˈkœntn̩ ˈʃtaɪ̯ɡən]
examples.translation: She thinks prices could go up.
examples.note: The modal 'könnten' expresses possibility in the summary.

examples.original: Anders ausgedrückt, das Problem ist nicht neu.
examples.phonetic: [ˈandɐs ˈaʊ̯sɡədʁʏkt, das pʁoˈbleːm ɪst nɪçt nɔʏ̯]
examples.translation: In other words, the problem isn’t new.
examples.note: Formula to introduce a paraphrase.

examples.original: Das heißt also, wir müssen unsere Strategie überdenken.
examples.phonetic: [das haɪ̯st ˈalzo, viːɐ̯ ˈmʏsn̩ ˈʊnzəʁə ʃtʁateˈɡiː yːbɐˈdɛŋkn̩]
examples.translation: That is to say, we need to reconsider our strategy.
examples.note: 'Das heißt' as a connector for reformulating.

title: Using idiomatic expressions naturally / Usar expresiones idiomáticas con naturalidad
bridge: In Spanish, idiomatic expressions are often translated literally between Romance languages, but in German many have fixed structures that do not match the Spanish ones. For example, 'tener algo en la punta de la lengua' in Spanish does not use the verb 'tener' in German, but 'liegen' (to lie). Additionally, German frequently uses modal verbs and particles that change the nuance. For a Spanish speaker, the biggest challenge is not to translate word for word, but to memorize the context and register (formal/informal) in which they are used.
rule: German idiomatic expressions are fixed phrases whose meaning cannot be deduced from the individual words. To use them naturally at level B2: 1) Memorize the exact structure, including articles and prepositions (e.g. 'auf der Zunge liegen' not 'auf die Zunge'). 2) Pay attention to the register: many are colloquial (umgangssprachlich) and are not used in formal writing. 3) The word order is flexible, but the conjugated verb always occupies the second position in main clauses; in subordinate clauses it goes at the end. 4) Some expressions have almost literal equivalents in Spanish (e.g. 'das ist nicht mein Bier' = 'that's not my problem'), but others do not (e.g. 'Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof' = 'I don't understand a thing'). 5) Modal verbs (können, müssen, etc.) combine with idiomatic expressions to add nuance (e.g. 'Das kann ich dir nicht sagen' – not idiomatic, but 'Das kannst du laut sagen' is). 6) At B2 level, students are expected to recognize and produce at least 20-30 common idiomatic expressions in everyday and work contexts.

The typical mistake Spanish speakers make is to translate 'that's not my problem' literally as 'das ist nicht mein Problem', which, although understandable, is not idiomatic. The correct idiomatic expression is 'nicht mein Bier' (literally: not my beer). To avoid the mistake, memorize expressions as blocks, not word by word. Another equally idiomatic alternative is 'nicht meine Sache' (not my thing).

examples.translation: It's a piece of cake.

examples.note: Frequently used in work contexts to indicate effort.

examples.original: Das ist ein zweischneidiges Schwert.

examples.translation: That's a double-edged sword.

examples.original: Er hat den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen.

examples.translation: You hit the nail on the head.

examples.translation: I'm in a bad mood / something has annoyed me.

examples.translation: That goes straight to my heart (it affects me deeply).

title: Academic and professional register: Konjunktiv I and formal formulas / Academic and professional register: Konjunktiv I and formal formulas
bridge: In Spanish, the subjunctive is used in subordinate clauses to express doubt, desire, or impersonality (e.g., 'Se dice que sea...'). In German, for academic and professional register, the Konjunktiv I (subjunctive I) is used in indirect speech and fixed formulas to convey information objectively and distantly. A common mistake is using the Konjunktiv II (which expresses unreality) instead of the I, or translating the Spanish subjunctive literally with 'würde', which sounds colloquial. Here you will learn to distinguish them and use the formulas required in formal contexts.
rule: The Konjunktiv I is primarily formed from the present stem: for most verbs, the 1st person plural form (wir) is taken and the endings -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en are added. Example: 'kommen' → 'er komme'. It is used in: 1) Indirect speech (indirekte Rede) to quote what someone has said without expressing your own opinion. 2) Instructions and recipes (but in professional register more in manuals). 3) Fixed formulas of politeness or impersonality: 'man nehme' (take), 'es sei darauf hingewiesen' (it should be noted). In professional and academic contexts, it is essential for minutes summaries, formal emails, and scientific texts. Exceptions: modal verbs and 'sein' have their own forms (e.g., 'er sei'). When the Konjunktiv I form coincides with the present indicative (especially in 1st and 3rd person plural, or with 'wir' and 'sie'), the Konjunktiv II is used as a substitute form (ersatz). In practice, at B2 level, the Konjunktiv I is mainly used in the 3rd person singular and in fixed formulas.

concept_examples.translation: The company announces that it is increasing prices.
concept_examples.phonetic: [diː ˈfɪʁma taɪ̯lt mɪt, das ziː diː ˈpʁaɪ̯zə ɛɐ̯ˈhøːə]

common_error.wrong: Der Professor sagt, dass die Studierenden die Prüfung bestehen würden.
common_error.correct: Der Professor sagt, die Studierenden hätten die Prüfung bestanden.
common_error.correct_alt: Der Professor sagt, die Studierenden bestünden die Prüfung.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because Spanish speakers tend to use 'würde + infinitive' to avoid the forms of the Konjunktiv II, but in indirect speech, the Konjunktiv I is correct, especially in formal register. Additionally, 'bestehen' in Konjunktiv II (bestünden) is more formal than its 'würde' variant. The confusion between Konjunktiv I and II is typical: Konjunktiv I is for quoting speech (objectivity), while Konjunktiv II is used for unreality or politeness. To avoid it, learn the Konjunktiv I forms of common verbs (haben, sein, werden, modals) and recognize when the form is ambiguous (e.g., 'sie haben' → 'sie haben' in Konjunktiv I, so 'sie hätten' is used) and only resort to Konjunktiv II in that case.

levels.label: Konjunktiv I im indirekten Rede (estilo indirecto)

examples.original: Er sagt, er komme morgen.
examples.phonetic: [eːɐ̯ zaːkt, eːɐ̯ ˈkɔmə ˈmɔʁɡn̩]
examples.translation: He says that he is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: In indirect speech, Konjunktiv I is used to indicate that it is someone else’s statement, not yours. In Spanish, the indicative is correct here, making this a key difference.

examples.original: Sie behauptet, sie habe das Problem gelöst.
examples.phonetic: [ziː bəˈhaʊ̯ptət, ziː ˈhaːbə das pʁoˈbleːm ˈɡəløːst]
examples.translation: She states that she has solved the problem.
examples.note: The form 'habe' is the Konjunktiv I of 'haben' and avoids ambiguity with the present. In Spanish, the indicative is correct.

examples.original: Die Forscher meinen, das Experiment sei erfolgreich gewesen.
examples.phonetic: [diː ˈfɔʁʃɐ ˈmaɪ̯nən, das ɛkspeʁiˈmɛnt zaɪ̯ ɛɐ̯ˈfɔlkʁaɪ̯ç ɡəˈveːzn̩]
examples.translation: The researchers believe that the experiment was successful.
examples.note: 'sei' is the Konjunktiv I form of 'sein'. It is used to convey a quoted opinion without verification.

examples.original: Es sei darauf hingewiesen, dass...
examples.phonetic: [ɛs zaɪ̯ ˈdaːʁaʊ̯f ˈhɪnɡəˌviːzn̩, das]
examples.translation: It should be noted that...
examples.note: Common impersonal formula in academic writing. In Spanish, 'hay que señalar' or 'se debe señalar' is used.

examples.original: Man beachte bitte die folgenden Hinweise.
examples.phonetic: [maːn bəˈaxtə ˈbɪtə diː ˈfɔlɡn̩dən ˈhɪnvaɪ̯zə]
examples.translation: Please take the following instructions into account.
examples.note: In professional contexts, 'man + Konjunktiv I' (man beachte) is an impersonal imperative form. In Spanish, the impersonal 'se' is used.

examples.original: Die Ergebnisse seien in der folgenden Tabelle zusammengefasst.
examples.phonetic: [diː ɛɐ̯ˈɡeːpnɪsə zaɪ̯n ɪn deːɐ̯ ˈfɔlɡn̩dən taˈbɛlə t͡suˈzamənɡəˌfast]
examples.translation: The results are summarized in the following table.
examples.note: Use of 'seien' (Konjunktiv I of 'sein') for impersonal instructions. In Spanish, the passive or impersonal voice is used.

levels.label: Konjunktiv II als Ersatzform (Sustitución por Konjunktiv II)
levels.translation: Konjunktiv II as a substitute form

examples.original: Sie sagten, sie hätten keine Zeit.
examples.phonetic: [ziː ˈzaːktn̩, ziː ˈhɛtən ˈkaɪ̯nə t͡saɪ̯t]
examples.translation: They said that they did not have time.
examples.note: When the Konjunktiv I is identical to the present (sie haben), the Konjunktiv II (hätten) is used to avoid ambiguity. Here 'hätten' is used instead of 'haben'.

examples.original: Er erklärte, er wäre krank gewesen.
examples.phonetic: [eːɐ̯ ɛɐ̯ˈkleːɐ̯tə, eːɐ̯ ˈvɛːʁə kʁaŋk ɡəˈveːzn̩]
examples.translation: He explained that he had been sick.
examples.note: Use of 'wäre' (Konjunktiv II of 'sein') as a substitute for the Konjunktiv I 'sei' when it is ambiguous.

examples.original: Man müsste die Daten erneut überprüfen.
examples.phonetic: [maːn ˈmʏstə diː ˈdaːtn̩ ɛɐ̯ˈnɔɪ̯t ʔyːbɐˈpʁyːfn̩]
examples.translation: The data should be reviewed again.
examples.note: In formal recommendations, the Konjunktiv II of 'müssen' (müsste) is used to soften the statement. In Spanish, 'habría que' has a similar nuance.
